items.title: “I don’t need to promise that on paper.”
items.where: Labels Are Descriptive, Not Prescriptive, P1
items.your_version: True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label we put on it. If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings and fears, then I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s an even more obvious red flag.

items.where: Reverting to babyhood, P1
items.your_version:
Reverting to babyhood
Relationship may activate wounds that were already there. Sometimes it may open a level of the heart that is simply very young and vulnerable, whether you knew there was a wound there or not. You become like a baby again. There’s a reason lovers call each other “baby.” And after all, Christ said "unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 18:3). Well, the Kingdom of Heaven may require extensive therapy to arrive at if being a baby was difficult the first time for either of us.

As mentioned with Bee, but also with Key, and H., there was always some sense that they were remembering how their dad treated them and judging me according to how close to him—or different from him—I was. That put me in a tough position. I want to play the role they need in some way, but I don’t want to hold onto the actual reality of me being me, with no need for putting on a show.

items.your_version:
Romance Shouldn’t Be Adjudicated

The moment I have to prove that I’m the man, something has already become fake, which I hate. Then it's like I have to defend the identity every time I'm not leading the way confidently & correctly, or god forbid if I need help or I cry!

I'm not really like that, and I do like to decide things together. Bee once called me her “wife” because of that. I don’t recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.  🫣

But I do have a masculine side, and when a woman appreciates that masculine side of me, it tends to come out by itself even more.

And women also shouldn't have to perform softness, or cute helplessness every minute to prove their femininity. Surrender means so much more when she *could* take control, but she doesn't, like an offering in trust. 

But in some sense, being the one who's supposed to be more childish can be even harder than having the more responsible gender role. She may worry that I don’t find her young and beautiful enough, or that she’s too emotional, difficult, and needy. Then she can over-correct, pulling back into needing nobody, and make receiving care or letting her man lead feel like weakness.

Toft says that after fifty years he still tells his wife she’s beautiful, including finding new kinds of beauty as she ages. 

Anami talks a lot about women needing to learn to receive a man's help, leadership, or attempts at giving her pleasure, without feeling like it costs them their agency. Sometimes that’s as ordinary as a woman who knows perfectly well how to drive asking me to drive, because she likes how it feels not to. 

As her man, I can help her come into her femininity by, for example, asking, “Honey, how do you see this intuitively?” And that's actually one of the powerful sides of femininity, so it can be a good bridge also if she's a bit stuck in masculine mode. And then she might ask me to help think through the practical side to life me up and help me shine.

That's the way we can invite each other to play our unique roles rather than huff and puff in disappointment. Would you rather go to a party where you were invited or a war you got drafted into?

When a woman doesn’t know how to gently invite a man to lead, she may manufacture a crisis until the man is forced to take charge to get the same outward result.

Unfortunately, I’ve seen a lot of the latter.

items.my_version: Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don’t use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex’s wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don’t use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him: looking honestly at your part doesn’t erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, “What would Mr. Rogers do?” (if you’re old enough to remember that show).

items.where: After leaving, P4
items.your_version: I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter, even if things ended on that bitter note. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. On the other hand, it can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You’re not a yo-yo.
